chapters.title: Never Outshine the Master
chapters.keys: Always make the people above you feel comfortably superior. If you show off your talents too much, you stir up their fear and insecurity and it backfires. Make your masters look more brilliant than they are, and you will rise. Reversal: If your master is already falling, you have nothing to fear from outshining him and need not be merciful, but if he is still firm, wait patiently until his power fades. Story Greene tells: Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's finance minister, threw a lavish party at his chateau that dazzled the court and showed up the king; within weeks he was arrested and spent the rest of his life in prison. Galileo dedicated his discovery of Jupiter's moons to the Medici family, making his patrons look glorious, and was rewarded with a secure post as their court philosopher and mathematician.

chapters.title: Never Put Too Much Trust in Friends, Learn How to Use Enemies
chapters.keys: Be wary of friends, because envy makes them quick to betray you and familiarity makes them spoiled and tyrannical. Hire a former enemy instead, because he has more to prove and will be more loyal. You have more to fear from friends than from enemies. If you have no enemies, find a way to make some. Reversal: A friend can be more useful than an enemy for dirty work or as a scapegoat, though sacrificing a friend costs you that friend for good. Story Greene tells: Byzantine emperor Michael III raised his friend Basil from stable hand to co-emperor and showered him with favor; Basil had him murdered and took the throne. The Song emperor Taizu persuaded the generals who had helped him to retire on comfortable pensions, and later won the loyalty of a defeated enemy ruler by treating him generously.

chapters.title: Conceal Your Intentions
chapters.keys: Never reveal the purpose behind what you do. People who have no clue what you are after cannot prepare a defense. Lead them down the wrong path and wrap them in enough smoke that they see your aim only when it is too late. Reversal: Once you are known as a deceiver, no smoke screen works, so openly play the honest or repentant rogue and you can keep running your schemes. Story Greene tells: The young Marquis de Sévigné, coached by the courtesan Ninon de Lenclos, kept revealing his feelings to the countess he was courting and lost her. Otto von Bismarck gave a speech supporting peace with Austria, the opposite of his real views, which won him a ministerial post he later used to pursue his actual aims.

chapters.title: Always Say Less Than Necessary
chapters.keys: The more you say, the more common and less in control you seem. Say less, and stay vague and open-ended, and even a banal remark will sound original. Powerful people impress and intimidate by holding back. Every extra word raises the chance of saying something foolish. Reversal: Silence can arouse suspicion, especially in your superiors, and sometimes you do better talking a lot like the court jester, using words to hide a deception and seem harmless. Story Greene tells: The Roman war hero Coriolanus kept insulting the common people in speeches when he ran for consul, lost their support, and was banished, after which he joined Rome's enemies. Louis XIV said very little at court, often answering only that he would see, which kept courtiers guessing and strengthened his authority.

chapters.title: So Much Depends on Reputation - Guard It with Your Life
chapters.keys: Reputation is the cornerstone of power. With it alone you can intimidate and win, and once it slips you are open to attack from all sides. Make yours unassailable and stop attacks before they happen. Learn to destroy enemies by opening holes in their reputations, then stand aside and let public opinion finish them. Reversal: There is none, because if you neglect your reputation you simply let others decide it for you. Story Greene tells: The Chinese strategist Zhuge Liang, caught with almost no troops, opened his city gates and sat calmly playing the lute; his rival Sima Yi, knowing his reputation for cunning, feared a trap and retreated. P. T. Barnum attacked the reputation of a rival museum through press campaigns and stunts until it lost its public and he took it over.

chapters.title: Court Attention at All Costs
chapters.keys: Everything is judged by appearance, and what goes unseen counts for nothing. Never get lost in the crowd. Stand out at all costs and make yourself a magnet for attention by seeming larger, more colorful and more mysterious than the timid masses. Reversal: As you rise you must keep changing your methods, because the same act wears the public out. Story Greene tells: P. T. Barnum built his fame with outrageous exhibits, hoaxes, and stunts that kept the public talking and paying to see his attractions. Margaretha Zelle reinvented herself in Paris as the exotic dancer Mata Hari, wrapping herself in mystery and becoming famous across Europe.

chapters.title: Get Others to Do the Work for You, but Always Take the Credit
chapters.keys: Use the wisdom, knowledge and legwork of other people to advance your own cause. It saves you time and energy and gives you an aura of godlike efficiency. Your helpers will be forgotten and you will be remembered. Never do yourself what others can do for you. Reversal: Taking the credit is unwise when your power is not yet secure or when you have a master above you, so know when sharing or giving up the credit serves you, as Kissinger did with Nixon over China. Story Greene tells: Nikola Tesla did inventive work that others, including Thomas Edison and Marconi, profited from or took credit for, and he died poor and largely unrecognized.

chapters.title: Make Other People Come to You - Use Bait If Necessary
chapters.keys: When you force the other person to act, you are the one in control. Make your opponent come to you and abandon his own plans in the process. Lure him with the prospect of fabulous gains, then attack. Reversal: Sometimes the opposite works better, and a sudden, aggressive first strike shocks and demoralizes the enemy. Story Greene tells: Talleyrand quietly helped make it possible for Napoleon to escape from exile on Elba and march back to power, drawing him into a fight on others' terms that ended at Waterloo and in permanent exile.

chapters.title: Win Through Your Actions, Never Through Argument
chapters.keys: Any win you get through argument is hollow, because the resentment outlasts the change of opinion. Get people to agree through your actions, without saying a word. Demonstrate, do not explain. Reversal: Argument is useful for distracting people and covering your tracks when you are deceiving them or caught in a lie, and then you should argue with all the conviction you can muster. Story Greene tells: A Roman military engineer argued with the consul Mucianus that a different mast would work better than the one ordered; the consul had him stripped and flogged to death. Michelangelo, told by Piero Soderini that David's nose was too big, pretended to chisel it while letting marble dust fall, and Soderini went away pleased.

chapters.title: Infection: Avoid the Unhappy and Unlucky
chapters.keys: Misery is infectious, and you can die from someone else's. You may think you are helping a drowning man, but you are only bringing on your own disaster. The unfortunate sometimes draw misfortune on themselves, and they will draw it on you too. Associate with the happy and fortunate instead. Reversal: There is none; the law applies universally, and ignoring it is at your peril. Story Greene tells: Lola Montez brought ruin to the men around her: the journalist Alexandre Dujarier was killed in a duel, and King Ludwig I of Bavaria lost his throne after his infatuation with her stirred unrest.

chapters.title: Learn to Keep People Dependent on You
chapters.keys: To stay independent you must always be needed and wanted. The more people rely on you, the more freedom you have. Make them depend on you for their happiness and prosperity. Never teach them enough to do without you. Reversal: Dependence runs both ways, and though you might try to stand alone by cornering everything as a monopolist does, that isolates you, so mutual dependence is the better position. Story Greene tells: The Poggio family of Lucca helped the condottiere Castruccio Castracani rise to power, and once he no longer needed them he had them executed. Bismarck made himself indispensable to the Prussian crown, so the king came to depend on him and his power grew.

chapters.title: Use Selective Honesty and Generosity to Disarm Your Victim
chapters.keys: One sincere, honest move will cover dozens of dishonest ones. Open-hearted honesty and generosity bring down the guard of even suspicious people. Once that opens a hole in their armor, you can deceive and manipulate them at will. A well-timed gift, a Trojan horse, does the same job. Reversal: If you have a history of deceit, sudden honesty or kindness only looks suspicious, so you are better off playing the rogue. Story Greene tells: The swindler Count Victor Lustig borrowed money from Al Capone and returned it untouched, claiming his deal had failed; Capone was so struck by his honesty that he gave Lustig a cash gift, which was what Lustig wanted all along.

chapters.title: When Asking for Help, Appeal to People's Self-Interest, Never to Their Mercy or Gratitude
chapters.keys: When you need help from an ally, do not remind him of your past good deeds, because he will find a way to ignore you. Find something in your request or your alliance that benefits him and emphasize it out of all proportion. He will respond eagerly when he sees something in it for himself. Reversal: Some powerful people find an appeal to self-interest ugly and want a public chance to show their charity and feel superior, so learn which kind you face and give those people that chance. Story Greene tells: In ancient Greece, Corinth asked Athens for support by appealing to past favors, while Corcyra pointed to what an alliance would gain Athens; Athens sided with Corcyra.

chapters.title: Pose as a Friend, Work as a Spy
chapters.keys: You must know about your rivals, so use spies to stay a step ahead. Better still, be the spy yourself. In polite social encounters, probe with indirect questions so people reveal their weaknesses and intentions. Every occasion is a chance for artful spying. Reversal: Others will spy on you too, so plant false information and surround your truth with lies to control the game. People in the story Greene tells here (from the checked chapter): Joseph Duveen, Andrew Mellon, London

chapters.title: Crush Your Enemy Totally
chapters.keys: A feared enemy must be crushed completely. Leave one ember burning and the fire will break out again. Stopping halfway loses more than total annihilation, because the enemy recovers and seeks revenge. Crush him in body and in spirit. Reversal: Sometimes it is better to leave a cornered enemy a way out or let him destroy himself, once you are sure he cannot recover, and though crushing someone can breed a long grudge, it is almost always wiser to crush him and do it again if he returns. Story Greene tells: Xiang Yu had his rival Liu Bang at his mercy and let him go; Liu Bang later defeated him, and Xiang Yu killed himself. Wu Zetian rose from concubine to ruler of China by eliminating every rival in her path, then ruled for decades.

chapters.title: Use Absence to Increase Respect and Honor
chapters.keys: The more you are seen and heard, the more common you appear. Once you are established in a group, withdraw for a time and you will be more talked about and more admired. Learn when to leave. Create value through scarcity. Reversal: This works only after you have reached a certain level of power through strong presence, because if you leave too early you are simply forgotten, so at the start make yourself seen everywhere. Story Greene tells: Deioces of Media made himself indispensable as a judge, then withdrew; as disorder grew, the people made him king, and he ruled while staying out of sight to keep his aura.

chapters.title: Keep Others in Suspended Terror: Cultivate an Air of Unpredictability
chapters.keys: People are creatures of habit who need to see familiar patterns in others, and your predictability gives them a sense of control. Turn that around and be deliberately unpredictable. Behavior with no apparent consistency keeps them off balance and wears them out trying to explain it. Taken to the extreme, it intimidates and terrorizes. Reversal: A familiar routine can lull people and serve as a cover for deception or set up a shocking break from the pattern, and too much unpredictability backfires, especially for a subordinate, by looking like indecision or instability. Story Greene tells: Bobby Fischer kept Boris Spassky off balance before and during their 1972 championship with erratic demands, delays, and odd moves, unsettling him and winning the title.

chapters.title: Do Not Build Fortresses to Protect Yourself - Isolation Is Dangerous
chapters.keys: A fortress seems the safest answer to a dangerous world, but isolation exposes you to more danger than it stops. It cuts you off from valuable information and makes you a conspicuous, easy target. Circulate among people and find allies. The crowd shields you from your enemies. Reversal: Isolation is almost never right, and its one use is short, small doses for clear thinking, keeping your way back into society open, because it breeds strange ideas and is hard to escape. Story Greene tells: Qin Shi Huangdi, the first emperor of China, walled himself away in his palaces, grew paranoid and out of touch, and died isolated while his ministers hid his death. Louis XIV did the opposite, keeping the nobility close at Versailles where he could see and control them.

chapters.title: Know Who You're Dealing With - Do Not Offend the Wrong Person
chapters.keys: People differ, so never assume everyone will react to your moves the same way. Deceive or outmaneuver the wrong person and he may spend his life seeking revenge. Some are wolves dressed as lambs. Choose your victims and opponents carefully, and never offend or deceive the wrong one. Reversal: There is none; ignorance about people gains you nothing, so learn to tell lions from lambs. Story Greene tells: The Shah of Khwarezm insulted Genghis Khan by killing his envoys, and the Mongols destroyed his empire. A Chinese prince, Chong'er, was treated with contempt by a ruler while in exile; when he later came to power he took his revenge on that state.

chapters.title: Do Not Commit to Anyone
chapters.keys: Only a fool rushes to take sides. Commit to no side or cause but yourself. Keep your independence and you become master of others, playing them against one another and making them pursue you. Reversal: Push this too far and people will see through you and gang up on you or lose interest, so at times commit to one side, at least for appearance, while keeping your inner independence. Story Greene tells: Queen Elizabeth I kept foreign suitors hoping for marriage but never committed, preserving her power and independence. Isabella d'Este kept her small state alive amid warring Italian powers by never firmly siding with any of them.

chapters.title: Play a Sucker to Catch a Sucker - Seem Dumber Than Your Mark
chapters.keys: No one likes feeling stupider than the next person. Make your victims feel smart, and smarter than you. Once they believe that, they will never suspect your motives. Reversal: Early in your climb you may need to show your bosses subtly that you are sharper than the competition, and a show of intelligence can sometimes cover a deception. Story Greene tells: Philip Arnold and John Slack salted a field with gems and posed as simple prospectors, fooling rich investors and experts into a fake diamond rush and walking away with a fortune.

chapters.title: Use the Surrender Tactic: Transform Weakness into Power
chapters.keys: When you are the weaker side, never fight for honor's sake. Surrender instead. It gives you time to recover, to torment and irritate your conqueror, and to wait for his power to fade. Surrender first and deny him the satisfaction of beating you, because turning the other cheek infuriates and unsettles him. Reversal: When the enemy will not be appeased, martyrdom is the opposite choice, but its effect is uncertain and you are not there to enjoy any power it brings, so surrender is usually better. Story Greene tells: The Melians refused to submit to Athens, and the Athenians killed their men and enslaved the rest. Bertolt Brecht, called before the House Un-American Activities Committee, appeared polite and cooperative while giving nothing away, then left the United States untouched.

chapters.title: Concentrate Your Forces
chapters.keys: Conserve your forces and energy by keeping them concentrated at their strongest point. You gain more by mining one rich mine deeper than by flitting between shallow ones. Intensity beats extensity. When you seek a source of power, find the one key patron who will keep feeding you for a long time. Reversal: The weaker side may do better to disperse, guerrilla-style, as Mao did, and tying yourself to one patron is dangerous if that patron falls, so in turbulent times several sources of power are wiser. Story Greene tells: The kingdom of Wu under Fu Chai spread its forces over too many conquests and was destroyed by its neighbor Yue. The Rothschild family kept their wealth and business tightly concentrated within the family and became a dominant banking power.

chapters.title: Play the Perfect Courtier
chapters.keys: A court runs on power and political skill, so master indirection. Flatter, yield to your superiors, and assert power over others in oblique, graceful ways. Do not show off, keep your flattery sparing, never bring bad news, never act like your master's friend, and never criticize those above you directly. Master these rules and there is no limit to how far you can rise at court. Reversal: You cannot please everyone, and your very success as a courtier will stir up envy and make enemies. Story Greene tells: The painter Jean-Baptiste Isabey, painting the Congress of Vienna, arranged the scene so neither Talleyrand nor Wellington appeared lesser, flattering both.

chapters.title: Re-Create Yourself
chapters.keys: Do not accept the role society hands you. Re-create yourself with a new identity that commands attention and never bores the audience. Be the master of your own image rather than letting others define it. Use dramatic devices in your public actions so you seem larger than life. Reversal: There is essentially none, because even seeming natural takes acting, and the only limit is to avoid overacting, which is simply bad theater. Story Greene tells: Julius Caesar shaped his public image through spectacle and theatrical gestures, making himself a figure the Roman crowd loved. Aurore Dupin created the persona of George Sand, adopting a man's name and dress to command attention and freedom in Parisian literary life.

chapters.title: Keep Your Hands Clean
chapters.keys: You must look civil and efficient, with hands never dirtied by mistakes or nasty deeds. Keep that spotless appearance by using others as scapegoats and cat's-paws to hide your involvement. Let someone else do the dirty work and take the blame. Reversal: Scapegoats and cat's-paws must be used with great care, because they are screens, and if one fails, your manipulation is exposed. Story Greene tells: Cesare Borgia had his lieutenant Remirro de Orco pacify the Romagna with brutal methods, then had him killed and displayed publicly, so the cruelty was blamed on Remirro.

chapters.title: Play on People's Need to Believe to Create a Cultlike Following
chapters.keys: People have an overwhelming desire to believe in something. Make yourself the focal point of that desire by offering them a cause or new faith. Keep your words vague but full of promise, and put enthusiasm ahead of clear thinking. Give your followers rituals and ask them to make sacrifices for you. Reversal: If the group sees through you, an angry crowd will tear you apart, so watch for doubt, keep your bags packed, and consider working on people one at a time, because one sucker is easier to escape. Story Greene tells: The Milanese alchemist Francesco Borri gathered a devoted following through mystical claims before he was eventually imprisoned. Franz Mesmer drew crowds with his theory of animal magnetism until an official commission discredited it.

chapters.title: Enter Action with Boldness
chapters.keys: If you are unsure of a course of action, do not attempt it, because your doubts will infect how you carry it out. Timidity is dangerous, so go in boldly. Mistakes made through audacity can be fixed with more audacity. Everyone admires the bold and no one honors the timid. Reversal: Boldness is a tool for the right moment after careful planning, not a way of life, as Lola Montez shows, and timidity is useful only when feigned to lure people in. Story Greene tells: Count Victor Lustig boldly posed as a government official and sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap to a dealer, who was too embarrassed to report the swindle.

chapters.title: Plan All the Way to the End
chapters.keys: The ending is everything. Plan all the way to it, accounting for every consequence, obstacle and twist of fortune that could undo your work or hand the glory to someone else. Do that and circumstances will not overwhelm you, and you will know when to stop. Reversal: Build in alternatives so a rigid plan does not trap you when fortune shifts, but more people lose through vagueness and improvising than through overplanning, so refusing to plan ahead does you no good. Story Greene tells: Vasco Núñez de Balboa discovered the Pacific without planning how to protect his gains, and he was executed by the rival governor Pedrarias. Bismarck planned his wars in sequence and stopped once his goals were met, uniting Germany under Prussia.

chapters.title: Make Your Accomplishments Seem Effortless
chapters.keys: Your actions must look natural and easy. Hide all the toil, practice and clever tricks behind them. Act as though you could do much more. Showing how hard you work only raises questions, and teaching your tricks lets people use them against you. Reversal: Your secrecy must seem lighthearted, because grim zeal in hiding your methods looks paranoid, and letting people see a little behind the curtain on your own terms can win you admiration. Story Greene tells: Harry Houdini made his escapes look effortless while hiding the training and preparation behind them, which made his fame and mystique.

chapters.title: Control the Options: Get Others to Play with the Cards You Deal
chapters.keys: The best deception gives the other person what looks like a choice. Victims feel in control while acting as your puppets. Offer options that all come out in your favor, or force a choice between two evils that both serve you. Put them on the horns of a dilemma so they are gored whichever way they turn. Reversal: Limiting others' options can limit your own, so sometimes give them some freedom and watch how they use it to gather information you can use against them later. Story Greene tells: Ivan the Terrible left Moscow and threatened to abdicate, and the people begged him to return on his terms, giving him near-absolute power. Empress Dowager Cixi kept control of China by placing child emperors on the throne and ruling through them.

chapters.title: Play to People's Fantasies
chapters.keys: People avoid the truth because it is ugly, so never appeal to reality unless you are ready for the anger that disenchantment brings. Life is so harsh that anyone who can manufacture romance or fantasy is like an oasis in the desert. Everyone flocks to that person. There is great power in tapping the fantasies of the masses. Reversal: Fantasy carries danger, because the audience half knows it is being fooled and plays along for amusement, so keep it light and do not go too far. Story Greene tells: The alchemist Bragadino arrived in Venice claiming to turn base metal into gold; the city poured money into him until it realized he could deliver nothing, and he was eventually executed.

chapters.title: Discover Each Man's Thumbscrew
chapters.keys: Everyone has a weakness, a gap in the castle wall. It is usually an insecurity, an uncontrollable emotion or need, or a small secret pleasure. Find it by watching gestures and unconscious signs. Once you have it, it is a thumbscrew you can turn to your advantage. Reversal: Playing on weaknesses can set off actions you cannot control, because people driven by emotion do not behave as your plans assume. Story Greene tells: Cardinal Richelieu worked on the weaknesses of Marie de' Medici and Louis XIII to rise to great power. The art dealer Joseph Duveen studied Andrew Mellon's wishes and vanity and won him as a major buyer.

chapters.title: Be Royal in Your Own Fashion: Act Like a King to Be Treated Like One
chapters.keys: How you carry yourself often determines how you are treated. Act vulgar or common and in the long run people will disrespect you. A king respects himself and inspires the same in others. Act regal and confident of your powers and you will seem destined for a crown. Reversal: Do not take it so far that you humiliate people or tower over the crowd as an easy target, and do not ignore the mood of the times, as Charles I did to his cost when people had turned against authority. Story Greene tells: Christopher Columbus, though of humble origins, carried himself like nobility and demanded titles and a share of profits, and the Spanish crown granted them. Louis-Philippe, the bourgeois king of France, acted like a common man and lost respect and eventually his throne in 1848.

chapters.title: Master the Art of Timing
chapters.keys: Never seem to be in a hurry, because hurrying shows you control neither yourself nor time. Always look patient, as if everything will come to you eventually. Study the moment and the spirit of the times for the trends that will carry you to power. Stand back when the time is not ripe and strike fiercely when it is. Reversal: There is no power in giving up control of time and drifting at its mercy. Story Greene tells: Joseph Fouché survived the French Revolution, Napoleon, and the restored monarchy by sensing when each regime was rising or falling and shifting his loyalty at the right moment.

chapters.title: Disdain Things You Cannot Have: Ignoring Them Is the Best Revenge
chapters.keys: When you acknowledge a petty problem, you give it existence and credibility. The more attention you pay an enemy, the stronger you make him. A small mistake often gets worse and more visible when you try to fix it, so sometimes leave it alone. If you want something you cannot have, show contempt for it, because the less interest you reveal, the more superior you seem. Reversal: Disdain must be used carefully, because some small troubles grow and fester if ignored, so learn to tell what is potentially disastrous from what is a mere irritant. Story Greene tells: After Pancho Villa raided New Mexico, the United States sent General Pershing's army chasing him through Mexico for months; it never caught him and only made him a bigger hero.

chapters.title: Create Compelling Spectacles
chapters.keys: Striking images and grand symbolic gestures create the aura of power, and everyone responds to them. Stage spectacles for those around you, full of arresting visuals and radiant symbols that heighten your presence. Dazzled by appearances, no one will notice what you are really doing. Reversal: Not sure what this chapter gives here, so nothing is stated. Story Greene tells: Cleopatra met Mark Antony on a gilded barge staged like a divine spectacle and won him over. Louis XIV built his image around the sun, using ceremony and symbols to make himself seem the center of everything.

chapters.title: Think as You Like but Behave Like Others
chapters.keys: Make a show of going against the times and people will think you want attention and look down on them. They will find a way to punish you for making them feel inferior. It is far safer to blend in and nurture the common touch. Share your originality only with tolerant friends and those sure to appreciate it. Reversal: Standing out pays only when your position is already secure and established, so your difference marks your distance from others.

chapters.title: Stir Up Waters to Catch Fish
chapters.keys: Anger and emotion work against your strategy, so always stay calm and objective. If you can make your enemies angry while you stay calm, you gain a decided advantage. Find the chink in their vanity, rattle them, and you hold the strings. Reversal: Be careful and study the enemy first, because some fish are best left at the bottom of the pond. Story Greene tells: Napoleon flew into a rage and insulted Talleyrand before others, while Talleyrand stayed calm; the outburst made Napoleon look weak, and Talleyrand went on to work against him.

chapters.title: Despise the Free Lunch
chapters.keys: What is offered free is dangerous, because it usually involves a trick or a hidden obligation. Pay your own way and you stay clear of gratitude, guilt and deceit. It is often wise to pay full price, because there is no cutting corners with excellence. Be lavish with money and keep it circulating, because generosity is a sign of power and a magnet for it. Reversal: Not sure what this chapter gives here, so nothing is stated.

chapters.title: Avoid Stepping into a Great Man's Shoes
chapters.keys: What comes first always looks better and more original than what follows. If you succeed a great man or have a famous parent, you must achieve double what they did to outshine them. Do not get lost in their shadow or stuck in a past you did not make. Change course, disparage the legacy of the overbearing father, and establish your own name. Reversal: A great predecessor's name can sometimes be exploited for its glamour, but that is a trick with limits and does not replace power of your own. Story Greene tells: Alexander the Great refused to live in the shadow of his father, Philip of Macedon, and set out on conquests far beyond his father's, making a name entirely his own.

chapters.title: Strike the Shepherd and the Sheep Will Scatter
chapters.keys: Trouble can often be traced to one strong individual: the stirrer, the arrogant underling, the poisoner of goodwill. Give such people room and others will fall under their influence. Do not wait and do not negotiate, because they are beyond redemption. Isolate or banish them, and when you strike the source of the trouble, the sheep will scatter. Reversal: Not sure what this chapter gives here, so nothing is stated.

chapters.title: Work on the Hearts and Minds of Others
chapters.keys: Coercion creates a reaction that eventually works against you. Seduce people into wanting to move in your direction, and a person you have seduced becomes your loyal pawn. Do it by working on their individual psychology and weaknesses. Soften the resistant by playing on what they hold dear and what they fear. Reversal: Not sure what this chapter gives here, so nothing is stated. Story Greene tells: Marie Antoinette ignored the feelings of the French people and became a hated symbol of royal excess; the Revolution sent her to the guillotine.

chapters.title: Disarm and Infuriate with the Mirror Effect
chapters.keys: A mirror reflects reality, but it is also a perfect tool of deception. Mirror your enemies by doing exactly what they do, and they cannot work out your strategy. It mocks and humiliates them and makes them overreact. Mirror their psyche and you seduce them with the illusion that you share their values, and mirror their actions and you teach them a lesson. Reversal: Pick your situations carefully, because mirroring can have consequences you did not plan for. People in the story Greene tells here (from the checked chapter): Alcibiades, Sparta, Athens, Persia, Tissaphernes

chapters.title: Preach the Need for Change, but Never Reform Too Much at Once
chapters.keys: Everyone agrees with change in the abstract, but day to day people are creatures of habit. Too much innovation is traumatic and leads to revolt. If you are new to power or an outsider building a base, make a show of respecting the old ways. If change is needed, make it feel like a gentle improvement on the past. Reversal: If the recent past was painful and bloody, do not associate yourself with it, as Napoleon knew when he set up a sober court unlike that of Louis XVI, so pay attention to the times. Story Greene tells: Thomas Cromwell pushed sweeping religious reform in England too far and too fast, provoking enemies and Henry VIII's displeasure, and was executed.

chapters.title: Never Appear Too Perfect
chapters.keys: Appearing better than others is always dangerous, and appearing to have no faults is the most dangerous of all. Envy creates silent enemies. Occasionally display defects and admit to harmless vices to deflect it and seem human and approachable. Only gods and the dead can seem perfect safely. Reversal: Not sure what this chapter gives here, so nothing is stated. People in the story Greene tells here (from the checked chapter): Cosimo de' Medici, Florence, Joe Orton, Kenneth Halliwell

chapters.title: Do Not Go Past the Mark You Aimed For; In Victory, Learn When to Stop
chapters.keys: The moment of victory is often the moment of greatest danger. Arrogance and overconfidence can push you past your goal, and going too far makes more enemies than you defeat. Do not let success go to your head. Set a goal, and when you reach it, stop. Reversal: Not sure what this chapter gives here, so nothing is stated. Story Greene tells: Cyrus the Great, after many victories, pressed on to invade the lands of Queen Tomyris and was killed. Madame de Pompadour held her place as Louis XV's favorite for years by not overreaching.

chapters.title: Assume Formlessness
chapters.keys: A shape or a visible plan opens you to attack. Give your enemy nothing to grasp, and stay adaptable and on the move. Accept that nothing is certain and no law is fixed. Be as fluid and formless as water, and never bet on stability or lasting order. Reversal: Formlessness is a tool for gaining power, not a go-with-the-flow attitude or resignation to fortune, and using it means seeing events for yourself and throwing out the laws and advice others preach. Story Greene tells: Mao Zedong fought Chiang Kai-shek by refusing set battles, dispersing and retreating, and outlasting his enemy until he won the civil war.
